tagline: Forests, river crossings and company-town history on Idaho’s timber-country roads
intro: The White Pine Scenic Byway crosses northern Idaho’s timber country, linking forests with marshland dotted by lakes fed by the lower Coeur d’Alene River. Visit Idaho presents this scenic byway as a journey through forests, rivers, mountains and historic sites, and gives the 80-mile drive a travel time of 1 hour, 38 minutes. Idaho 3 includes Mission Hill Creek Grade and Black Rock Grade, as well as stretches along and across the Coeur d’Alene River.

At St. Maries, Joseph Fisher chose a townsite southwest of two rivers’ meeting for a sawmill first built in 1889. Water carried logs to the mills and steamboats took finished lumber to market. Farther south, Potlatch grew as a company town serving a remote mill beside the company’s white pine holdings. In 2011, Idaho’s legislature gave Idaho 3 another identity, designating it the North Idaho Medal of Honor Highway.

Begin at I-90 and follow Idaho 3 south along and across the Coeur d’Alene River. Medimont sits on Cave Lake’s north shore; farther south, the road crosses the St. Joe River into St. Maries. Continue to Idaho 6 and turn southwest, passing Emida before reaching Harvard on the Palouse River. Harvard lies eight miles east of Potlatch on Idaho 6; the byway finishes at U.S. 95 at Potlatch.

moments.title: Old Mission State Park
moments.text: The Mission of the Sacred Heart was built without nails, using wattle and daub. Completed in 1853, it is Idaho’s oldest standing building. Antonio Ravalli designed the church, and Indigenous people constructed it. The mission later supplied travelers on the Mullan Road and served boats on the Coeur d’Alene River. Its parish house is a separate chapter: rebuilt in 1887 after a fire, it contains a smaller chapel. The park preserves both buildings and the surrounding property. A major restoration of the church was chosen as Idaho’s Bicentennial Project in 1976 to mark the nation’s bicentennial.

moments.title: Harvard
moments.text: Harvard’s name began with a refused honor. When the Washington, Idaho and Montana Railway reached this point in 1906, the community was founded beside the Palouse River. The railroad intended to name it Canfield after landowner Homer Canfield, but he suggested Harvard instead. That would complement Princeton, five miles west, whose own name came from Princeton, Minnesota. Harvard remains a community on Idaho 6, eight miles east of Potlatch, with a post office dating to 1906. Nearby names include Cornell, Vassar and Yale, though some collegiate matches were intentional and others coincidental.

moments.title: Potlatch
moments.text: Potlatch’s lumber company supplied houses as well as jobs. Crews began building the world’s largest white pine sawmill here in 1904, close to the company’s timber holdings. The company built 143 houses in 1906 and allowed only married couples to rent its homes. The mill closed in August 1981 as the economy and lumber prices declined. The commercial historic district includes its administrative office, which became city hall in the 1950s, and the 1906 railway depot, the town’s first major completed building. The district’s gymnasium has a porch on three sides supported by 16 Doric columns.
